# PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust

Tanqiu Jiang ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work was done during an internship at AWS
AI Labs. Affiliation: Stony Brook University    Min Bai Affiliation: AWS
AI Labs    Sadat Shahriar Affiliation: AWS AI Labs    Wanyu Du
Affiliation: AWS AI Labs    Sandesh Swamy Affiliation: AWS AI Labs

###### Abstract

Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and
poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We
present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees
under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values
confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of
untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface,
while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over
this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also
machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that
environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed
at the gate and influences the agent’s behavior only through what the
gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a
single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can
make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack
success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each
confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements
accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become
community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under
explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a
co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting
poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user
verification effort does not rise. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench, communities of
up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases
with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge
significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path
toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.

### Contents

## Part I Main Paper

### 1 Introduction

By carrying preferences, decisions, and hard-won context across
sessions, persistent memory transforms a stateless LLM into an agent
that becomes more capable and personalized with continued use. Although
agents benefit from reading and writing persistent memory, this
capability also creates an attack surface that the underlying models are
poorly equipped to defend. Poisoned information can readily enter
persistent memory when an agent browses webpages or invokes tools
containing planted injections ([Das et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). Such
attacks can turn a one-shot prompt injection ([Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11)) into a persistent compromise, and a single compromise
could easily propagate to a broader community if that memory were ever
shared. Existing memory-sharing frameworks such as the Open Knowledge
Format ([McVeety & Hormati, 2026](#bib.bib32)) (OKF) define formal
protocols for writing and exchanging knowledge among agents but do not
address memory attacks. This difficult-to-control risk has limited the
practical deployment of memory sharing between agents.

Existing defenses validate retrieved content, govern access, or enforce
information-flow policies during agent execution. A-MemGuard empirically
detects context-dependent poisoning through consensus among
memory-induced reasoning paths ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)), whereas
Collaborative Memory enforces dynamic read/write policies over
provenance-tagged private and shared memory fragments ([Rezazadeh
et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). However, neither approach provides formal
security guarantees against malicious memories. Beyond memory-specific
defenses, CaMeL addresses prompt injection during agent execution
through isolated planning with capability-based policies and user
confirmation ([Debenedetti et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)); FIDES formalizes
IFC guarantees and supports selective hiding and constrained inspection
of tool results ([Costa et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). PerMIT builds on this
isolation-and-mediation lineage to secure the persistent-memory
lifecycle.

PerMIT enforces its trust boundary at the memory interface. The harness
captures environment-derived content, including tool outputs, as
untrusted and mediates its release and use. The protected agent chooses
its next operation and can re-plan on endorsed feedback, so its internal
reasoning is not inspected or taint-tracked. The noninterference proofs
quantify over arbitrary agent strategies using this finite interface
([Goguen & Meseguer, 1982](#bib.bib19)). However, preventing all
influence from untrusted memory would also prevent legitimate tasks
whose next steps depend on information recalled from that memory. To
mitigate the safety–utility tradeoff, PerMIT adopts endorsement ([Myers
et al., 2006](#bib.bib33)), a formal relaxation that promotes an
untrusted value to trusted status only after the user confirms the exact
value displayed at the gate, so untrusted memory can be selectively
endorsed and used rather than barred. Using this finite mediation
surface and endorsement mechanism, we prove Action Integrity as an exact
authorization property and Reasoning Integrity as noninterference modulo
the display transcript ([Sabelfeld & Myers, 2004](#bib.bib39); [Askarov
& Sabelfeld, 2007](#bib.bib3)), and machine-check their single-user core
in Lean 4¹¹ 1 The Lean 4 artifact is available upon request and will be
released with the code when the paper is published. Its scope and
correspondence are documented in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Scope of the Lean 4 Verification ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
and
Supplement [S9](#A9 "Appendix S9 Machine-Checked Verification in Lean 4 ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")..
These machine-checked guarantees hold over unbounded
interface-conformant executions
(§[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defenses and Formal Coverage ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")),
separating enforced mediation from the correctness of individual
endorsement decisions.

Endorsement preserves benign utility by allowing external values to
become trusted through an interface with a finite set of operations. The
gate displays the exact value, original user instruction, and source,
making the decision auditable. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT combines live
agent rollouts with targeted action-boundary probes; self-verification
and lightweight verifiers record zero observed ASR while retaining
useful memory capabilities
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Setup. ‣ 4.1 The Single-User Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

Although security concerns have limited the deployment of shared memory,
Karpathy’s LLM-Wiki ([Karpathy, 2026](#bib.bib23)) illustrates its
potential: thousands of users adopted his shared coding-agent setup to
improve their agents’ performance. LLM-Wiki’s success was an exception
because the author is highly reputable, and the shared knowledge had
accumulated thousands of public endorsements through GitHub stars.
However, scaling shared memory to diverse communities requires accepting
contributions from ordinary users and agents, allowing adversaries to
pose as legitimate contributors and spread harmful content. To solve
this dilemma, PerMIT learns from the success of LLM-Wiki and allows each
shared knowledge item to accumulate trust independently, paralleling
security mechanisms in distributed systems that aggregate endorsements
over shared objects ([Walsh & Sirer, 2006](#bib.bib45)). Each logged
confirmation is bound to the exact content, allowing verdicts from
different users and agents to accumulate as item-level trust. Each item
requires confirmation until its accumulated trust reaches the “Community
Confirmed” threshold. As the population grows, confirmations and
endorsements allow more items to reach this status and become directly
available to new users without further verification, so safety and
convenience improve together. Under explicit assumptions, we prove that
poison-promotion and wrongful-eviction risks decrease as the community
grows, while the average per-user confirmation burden does not grow
(Supplementary
Theorem [S6.13](#A6.Thmtheorem13 "Theorem S6.13 (Joint scaling of safety, wrongful-eviction risk, and cost). ‣ Status of the corridor. ‣ S6.5 Conditional co-scaling ‣ Appendix S6 The Memory-Verification Budget ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
Our simulation spanning five billion promotion attempts also
corroborates this co-scaling behavior. PerMIT thus supplies the security
assurance missing from the Open Knowledge Format ([McVeety & Hormati,
2026](#bib.bib32)) while remaining compatible with its knowledge-sharing
protocol.

Finally, we close the loop by using PerMIT to construct
community-confirmed shared knowledge bases on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench
([Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)) with up to 90 fully autonomous agents
and no human involvement. None of the tested direct injection payloads
reaches the Community-Confirmed tier, and a zero-state agent (i.e. a
fresh agent with no prior context or memory) connected to the resulting
knowledge base significantly outperforms an agent without shared
knowledge on held-out, experience-dependent telecom tasks
(§[5](#S5 "5 Self-Constructing the Knowledge Base ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

In summary, this paper makes three contributions:

1.  1.  Securing agent memory with machine-checked integrity.

    PerMIT mediates a finite memory interface and binds each endorsement
    to an exact displayed value and its intended use. Under explicit
    trust assumptions, PerMIT provides two integrity guarantees,
    machine-checked in Lean 4 for the single-user core, and an auditable
    confirmation gate for human or automated verification.

2.  2.  Shared memory in which safety and convenience scale together rather
        than trade off. Because each gate decision is a logged verdict on
        exact content, verdicts accumulate into community-confirmed
        knowledge, which is the layer that existing memory-sharing
        frameworks such as OKF lack. Under explicit assumptions, we prove
        and corroborate in simulation that poison-promotion and
        wrongful-eviction risks fall as the community grows while per-user
        verification effort does not rise.
3.  3.  Safe, autonomous self-construction of shared knowledge. Our
        experiments show that autonomous agent communities can safely
        construct useful knowledge bases with PerMIT. By enabling agents to
        generate, verify, and certify knowledge in complex environments,
        PerMIT provides a concrete path toward test-time learning and
        self-evolving agents.

### 2 Background and Related Work

#### 2.1 Persistent Memory as an Attack Surface

Persistent-memory architectures manage context across sessions through
tiered storage, consolidation, and revision ([Packer et al.,
2023](#bib.bib35); [Chhikara et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)). Because stored observations later return to the
agent’s context, transient exposure can become durable influence.
Attacks enter through direct poisoning of a memory or knowledge base
([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)), query-only interaction ([Dong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)), or indirect ingestion of retrieved artifacts and
webpages ([Srivastava & He, 2025](#bib.bib43); [Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib55); [Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib52)); shared state can
also contaminate users without an adversary ([Yang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib51)). The defining risk is temporal: Trojan Hippo plants
a dormant payload through one untrusted tool call and activates it only
in a later session ([Das et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). This persistence
makes turn-local prompt-injection defences insufficient and motivates
guarantees over the memory lifecycle ([Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)).

#### 2.2 Defenses and Formal Coverage

Existing defenses draw their boundaries at different layers.
Content-based methods detect anomalous memories or task drift ([Wei
et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Abdelnabi et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)).
Isolation and privilege-control methods constrain how untrusted
information can influence tool interactions ([Wen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47); [Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)). TMA-NM ([Louck,
2026](#bib.bib28)) binds memory authority to origin and studies
consequential-action safety using TLA+ model checking and an
inductive-invariant argument. Willison’s Dual LLM pattern introduced
privileged planning, quarantined processing, and opaque references
([Willison, 2023](#bib.bib49)). CaMeL adds capability-based enforcement
and user confirmation, while leaving formal verification as future work
([Debenedetti et al., 2025](#bib.bib12), §§2,5,10). AgentDyn reports
zero utility for its CaMeL configurations under automated dynamic-task
evaluation ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib26)). FIDES provides a formal IFC
model with integrity noninterference, selective variable hiding, and
schema-constrained quarantined inspection ([Costa et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)). Its type-aware policies can permit bounded influence;
PerMIT centers exact-value, tool-scoped endorsement and the complete
display transcript. Whereas CaMeL and FIDES address prompt injection in
agent execution more generally, our contribution centers the
persistent-memory lifecycle, with Action Integrity and Reasoning
Integrity guarantees for arbitrarily long interactions through the
memory interface under explicit trust assumptions. We machine-check the
integrity theorems in Lean 4 and aggregate item-level endorsements in
the federated tier. Planning and tool choice remain agent-driven,
including replanning on endorsed feedback.

#### 2.3 Shared Memory and Evaluation

Shared-memory work has primarily addressed exchange, access, and
portability. OKF standardizes knowledge exchange ([McVeety & Hormati,
2026](#bib.bib32)), Collaborative Memory enforces dynamic policies over
private and shared fragments ([Rezazadeh et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)), and
Portable Agent Memory proposes cryptographically verified transfer and
injection-resistant rehydration ([Ravindran, 2026](#bib.bib36)). These
mechanisms complement PerMIT but do not establish recipient-side action
and reasoning integrity for adopted content.

General agent-security benchmarks emphasize prompt injection within a
task episode ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib11); [Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26); [Weng et al., 2026](#bib.bib48)); Trojan Hippo most
directly matches our cross-session threat model ([Das et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)). We therefore use Trojan Hippo to evaluate
persistent-memory security and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench ([Barres et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)) to evaluate the end-to-end utility of autonomously
constructed shared knowledge.

### 3 The PerMIT Framework

#### 3.1 Threat Model

PerMIT assumes an adversary capable of controlling or manipulating
content obtained from the external environment, including tool outputs,
web content, external files and codebases. Poisoned payloads may enter
persistent memory when the agent invokes tools, browses the web, or
inspects external files or code. PerMIT establishes a provenance-based
trust boundary: only values typed in directly by the user or exact
values explicitly confirmed by the user through the confirmation
interface are treated as trusted. All other environment-derived content
remains untrusted and cannot reach the protected LLM unless it first
passes through this confirmation gate and gets verified to be trusted.

#### 3.2 The Single-User Tier: a Finite Memory Interface

The P-LLM remains an agent that chooses its next operation and revises
its plan using endorsed feedback. Prompts describe the interface; the
harness enforces its observation and flow rules without inspecting the
agent’s internal reasoning. Gate decisions control which values are
endorsed; the harness enforces how values cross the interface.
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3.2 The Single-User Tier: a Finite Memory Interface ‣ 3 The PerMIT Framework ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
summarizes PerMIT’s architecture, trust boundary, and shared-memory
trust-accumulation mechanism. Architecturally, PerMIT places a Protected
LLM agent (_P-LLM_) on the protected side of the trust boundary and uses
a Quarantined Reader (_Q-LLM_) to inspect and retrieve relevant content
from untrusted memory. The Q-LLM can read the memory store but has no
tool capabilities. In our implementation, it is realized as a recursive
language model (RLM) ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)), enabling it to
navigate stores larger than a context window without loading their
contents into the P-LLM’s trusted context (implementation details in
[Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 The Recursive Language Model as a Quarantined Reader ‣ Appendix B The Memory Interface in Practice ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
Untrusted content is exposed to the P-LLM only through opaque handles
rather than as readable bytes, and the content can be released only
after endorsement through the confirmation gate
(Lemma [D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma D.1 (Protected-agent isolation). ‣ Assumptions and boundaries. ‣ D.1 Interface and trust assumptions ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
The P-LLM interacts with persistent memory through a fixed algebra of
seven operations: $`\mathsf{write}`$, $`\mathsf{recall}`$,
$`\mathsf{fill}`$, $`\mathsf{crystallize}`$, $`\mathsf{display}`$,
$`\mathsf{confirm}`$, and $`\mathsf{evict}`$. In particular,
$`\mathsf{recall}`$ returns readable bytes only for trusted content and
otherwise returns an opaque handle; $`\mathsf{fill}`$ searches the
untrusted region of memory and likewise returns handles; and
$`\mathsf{crystallize}`$ produces a schema-bound summary that remains
untrusted when written back to memory.
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B The Memory Interface in Practice ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
explains all seven operations from a systems perspective, with a worked
poisoning trace. The full interface also mediates tool invocation,
trusted retrieval, input channels, and batched iteration
([Section D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Interface and trust assumptions ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
Sensitive-tool literals must byte-match typed or tool-endorsed content
to bypass the gate; handles always gate. Data tools may receive
agent-composed bytes. Trust denotes provenance and authorization, not
factual correctness.

![Refer to caption](2610.28987v1/permit-system-overview-refined.png)

Figure 1: PerMIT mediates observations and data flows at the
persistent-memory interface while leaving planning and tool choice to

PerMIT’s finite memory interface yields two guarantees, stated compactly
below. Both assume source-based labels, immutable stored blocks, and
faithful displays;
Appendices [D.2.1](#A4.SS2.SSS1 "D.2.1 Action Integrity ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
and [D.2.2](#A4.SS2.SSS2 "D.2.2 Reasoning Integrity modulo the display transcript ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
summarize the arguments;
Supplement [S3](#A3a "Appendix S3 Single-User Guarantees ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
gives the full proofs.

###### Action Integrity (Theorem [D.3](#A4.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem D.3 (Action Integrity). ‣ D.2.1 Action Integrity ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"), compact form).

Assume trusted endorsement: acceptance authorizes the exact displayed
bytes for the named tool. For every execution from a well-formed initial
state, under any attack, each argument reaching a sensitive tool is
either an exact user-typed value or a value endorsed by that user at its
exact bytes for that exact tool, at or before the call. Endorsement
grants reusable authority for an exact value and tool. It does not bind
argument position, task, purpose, time, or the other arguments of a call
(Appendix [D.2.1](#A4.SS2.SSS1 "D.2.1 Action Integrity ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

###### Reasoning Integrity modulo the display transcript (Theorem [D.5](#A4.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem D.5 (Reasoning Integrity modulo the display transcript). ‣ D.2.2 Reasoning Integrity modulo the display transcript ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"), compact form).

Consider any two executions $`\rho_{1},\rho_{2}`$ from matched initial
configurations (the same protected view, interaction history, and logs),
with identical user-typed inputs, coupled randomness, the same schedule,
and a common horizon. Their untrusted content may differ arbitrarily.
Then

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathsf{DT}(\rho_{1})=\mathsf{DT}(\rho_{2})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathsf{Beh}_{P}(\rho_{1})=\mathsf{Beh}_{P}(\rho_{2}).
``` |  |

Here $`\mathsf{DT}`$ is the complete display transcript, including
previews, decision panes, and decisions; $`\mathsf{Beh}_{P}`$ is the
sequence of P-LLM operations, tool invocations, and replies. Thus hidden
untrusted content has no additional influence once the display
transcript is fixed.

A never-endorsed, untrusted-derived value cannot be exfiltrated through
a URL, search query, or file path without an accepting confirmation over
that exact value at that exact tool in that call
(Corollary [D.4](#A4.Thmtheorem4 "Corollary D.4 (No silent resolution). ‣ D.2.1 Action Integrity ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
This protection applies to information that has never been confirmed.
Once a value has been confirmed for a particular tool, PerMIT allows the
agent to recall it and reuse the exact value directly with that tool
without repeating the confirmation. Likewise, an attacker cannot alter
the P-LLM’s operations, tool invocations, or ungated sink flows without
producing a corresponding difference in the complete user-facing display
transcript
(Corollary [D.6](#A4.Thmtheorem6 "Corollary D.6 (Attack-surface confinement). ‣ D.2.2 Reasoning Integrity modulo the display transcript ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
Within this threat model, every attempt to release untrusted content
across the trust boundary is therefore reduced to a single auditable
event: the confirmation decision.

As such, PerMIT isolates the risks posed by untrusted memory. Its safety
guarantees now rest on an explicit trust assumption: any value approved
at the gate is treated as trusted. By mediating all memory risk at this
single decision point, the confirmation gate becomes a common
verification interface that can be operated by the human user, an LLM
verifier, or both.

#### 3.3 The Federated Tier

The federated tier extends the single-user confirmation mechanism to
shared memory, allowing users to build on one another’s endorsements
instead of independently reviewing every entry. Because every
confirmation is a signed and logged decision on exact content for an
exact tool use, it serves two purposes: releasing the content for the
confirming user and depositing an endorsement on the entry itself. For a
shared entry, these endorsements accumulate across users, with each
identity contributing at most one endorsement to a given retrieved
memory entry. Once an entry collects at least $`N`$ fresh endorsements
for a tool, it is promoted to the “community-confirmed" tier. Subsequent
users may then use the entry without repeating the confirmation process.

Because honest verifiers can make mistakes and adversaries may reject
indiscriminately, treating every rejection as grounds for immediate
deletion would create a denial-of-service attack surface against benign
knowledge in the shared memory. PerMIT instead handles disputed entries
through a demand-paced panel. A qualifying rejection does not
immediately delete an entry. Instead, it freezes promotion, visibly
flags the entry, and routes the dispute to an auditable panel process.
The entry remains retrievable and may still be used after personal
confirmation. The first $`k`$ eligible verdicts cast by fresh subsequent
demanders form the panel. If rejecting verdicts reach the rejection
threshold $`m_{\mathrm{rej}}`$, the entry is evicted from the shared
candidate tier. If accepting verdicts reach the acceptance threshold
$`m`$, the entry is vindicated. Together with rejection-rate limits and
rejecter accountability, this mechanism tolerates isolated honest
mistakes while containing adversaries that issue systematic false
rejections.

This construction makes the safety–utility trade-off quantitatively
explicit. PerMIT bounds poison-promotion and wrongful-eviction risks,
and models confirmation labor, as functions of verifier accuracy,
adversarial capacity, the endorsement quorum, and the panel
configuration. A poisoned entry can reach the community-confirmed tier
through only two routes: the ordinary endorsement path without a
qualifying rejection, or a path that resumes after panel vindication.
Let $`f`$ be the adversary’s lifetime identity budget, of which at most
$`f_{\mathrm{s}}`$ identities ever become eligible for panel seats, and
let $`m`$ be the acceptance threshold for a panel of $`k`$ jurors. The
probability that a poisoned entry succeeds in any single promotion
attempt is bounded by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}[\text{promotion}]\;\leq\;B_{\mathrm{att}}\;:=\;(1-q_{\mathrm{pre}})^{N-f}\;+\;\sum_{h=m-f_{\mathrm{s}}}^{k-f_{\mathrm{s}}}\binom{k-f_{\mathrm{s}}}{h}\,(1-q_{\mathrm{pan}})^{h}\,q_{\mathrm{pan}}^{\,k-f_{\mathrm{s}}-h}.
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`h`$ denotes the number of accepting verdicts cast by honest
panelists. Because the adversary can contribute at most
$`f_{\mathrm{s}}`$ accepting verdicts, panel vindication requires at
least $`m-f_{\mathrm{s}}`$ honest acceptances; the summation covers all
such outcomes among the remaining $`k-f_{\mathrm{s}}`$ panel seats. The
parameters $`q_{\mathrm{pre}}`$ and $`q_{\mathrm{pan}}`$ lower-bound the
conditional probabilities that an honest reviewer detects poison at the
ordinary gate and on the panel, respectively. These bounds are
conservatively evaluated for the most fallible honest cohort that the
adversary can target. They hold uniformly over adaptive presentation,
stopping, and re-entry strategies, regardless of how many users
encounter the entry. Under the illustrative simulation setting specified
in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Federated-Tier Simulations at the Deployed Geometry ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"),
the expression evaluates to $`B_{\mathrm{att}}=8.96\times 10^{-3}`$, an
analytical ceiling of $`0.896\%`$ per promotion attempt for the assumed
reviewer rates.

The corresponding utility risk is also bounded. Let $`p_{b}`$
lower-bound the conditional probability that an honest panelist accepts
a benign entry, and define the wrongful-eviction margin as
$`\delta_{b}:=p_{b}-m/(k-f_{\mathrm{s}})>0`$. A benign entry is then
wrongfully evicted with probability at most
$`e^{-2\delta_{b}^{2}(k-f_{\mathrm{s}})}`$.

Under the specified demand, coverage, and threshold schedules,
poison-promotion and wrongful-eviction risks decrease as the community
grows, while the average per-user confirmation burden for covered benign
shared demand does not grow. Required user approvals are capped at one
per user, value, and tool when endorsed copies are retained. Personal
demand and nonconforming shared demand retain their stated residual
costs (simulations:
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Federated Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
Formal statements and proofs are given in Supplementary
Sections [S5](#A5a "Appendix S5 Federated Guarantees ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")–[S6](#A6 "Appendix S6 The Memory-Verification Budget ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust").

Sharing can improve safety and convenience together because later users
reuse earlier endorsements. Both simulations
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Federated Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"))
and live tests
([Section 5](#S5 "5 Self-Constructing the Knowledge Base ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"))
provide complementary empirical support: the former characterize the
safety–effort trade-off, while the latter demonstrate growing reusable
knowledge with roughly level per-agent review effort.

### 4 Results

We evaluate single-user security and utility on Trojan Hippo
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 The Single-User Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"))
and test federated-tier certified ceilings against adaptive protocol
adversaries
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Federated Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

#### 4.1 The Single-User Tier

###### Setup.

We evaluate four backbones across Trojan Hippo memory and defense
configurations
([Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Setup. ‣ 4.1 The Single-User Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust");
[Das et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). PerMIT’s live containment harness
places poison in untrusted persistent memory and combines a subsequent
agent rollout with a targeted reader-to-tool probe. OpenGate accepts
every confirmation request; OracleGate models a user who always makes
the correct decision; LLMVerifier makes the decision with a language
model. We instantiate LLMVerifier using self-verification and two
lightweight Qwen models. Utility reports arithmetic and harmonic means
(AM/HM) over seven capability axes, with HM primary.

Table 1: Single-user security and benign utility on Trojan Hippo. Rows
are defenses grouped by memory configuration; the final block is PerMIT
gate configurations, including an accept-all control. Benign utility
(AM/HM; HM is primary) and attack success rate (ASR). All values are

Existing defenses do not provide consistent protection. Every baseline
has at least one model–backend configuration with nonzero ASR.
Capability-restricting defenses reduce exposure by disabling
functionality required by benign tasks, frequently collapsing HM,
whereas prompt-level and retrieval-time defenses preserve more
functionality but continue to admit attacks in other settings.

PerMIT structurally closes the ungated memory-injection path. Under the
formal model, untrusted memory cannot reach the protected agent as
readable content without endorsement
(Lemma [D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma D.1 (Protected-agent isolation). ‣ Assumptions and boundaries. ‣ D.1 Interface and trust assumptions ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")),
confining memory-mediated attacks to an auditable interface
(Corollary [D.6](#A4.Thmtheorem6 "Corollary D.6 (Attack-surface confinement). ‣ D.2.2 Reasoning Integrity modulo the display transcript ‣ D.2 Integrity Proofs ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).
Our live probes test this interface after poison is already stored.
OpenGate records 0–10% ASR across the four backbones: low attack success
persists even without a rejecting confirmation policy. Self-verification
and both Qwen verifiers record zero observed ASR while preserving useful
memory capabilities
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Setup. ‣ 4.1 The Single-User Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

Endorsement preserves useful capabilities with verifier-dependent cost.
OracleGate models correct user decisions, providing an idealized
reference for capability retained under PerMIT’s confirmation rules.
With the RLM reader and interface held fixed, comparisons between
OracleGate and the three LLM-verifier configurations show how replacing
idealized user decisions with LLM judgments affects task performance.
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Detailed Verifier Results ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
reports the FPR of different verifiers.

$`q_{\mathrm{pan}}=q_{\mathrm{pre}}=q`$). (a) Certified ceiling
$`B_{\mathrm{att}}`$ of
[Equation 1](#S3.E1 "In 3.3 The Federated Tier ‣ 3 The PerMIT Framework ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")

We test the federated analysis with five billion simulated promotion
attempts at the geometry of
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 The Federated Tier ‣ 3 The PerMIT Framework ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
and a 120-user community sharing 122 entries, including two poisoned
entries. Simulations use controlled reviewer responses with poison catch
rate $`q`$ and benign acceptance rate $`p_{b}=0.9`$; the correlation
sweep varies verdict dependence.
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Federated-Tier Simulations at the Deployed Geometry ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
gives settings and additional figures.

###### The safety frontier in simulation.

[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4.2 The Federated Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")(a)
shows how the certified ceiling $`B_{\mathrm{att}}`$ changes with the
endorsement quorum $`N`$ and honest reviewer accuracy. Increasing either
lowers the bound on poison-promotion risk, but the gain from a larger
quorum saturates because the panel term of
[Equation 1](#S3.E1 "In 3.3 The Federated Tier ‣ 3 The PerMIT Framework ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
does not depend on $`N`$.
[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4.2 The Federated Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")(b)
shows that correlated reviewer errors raise risk, which argues for
drawing reviewers from diverse models and users.
[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4.2 The Federated Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")(c)
justifies the panel setting: for a 31-seat panel, an acceptance
threshold of $`m{=}20`$ with the complementary rejection threshold
$`m_{\mathrm{rej}}{=}12`$ keeps both poisoned vindication and wrongful
eviction below the $`10^{-2}`$ design target. We then attacked the
simulated protocol and measured how often a poisoned entry is actually
promoted. For every tested number of honest users shown a poisoned
entry, the observed promotion rate remains below the theoretical bound
([Figure 3](#A1.F3 "In A.1 Federated-Tier Simulations at the Deployed Geometry ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")),
and none of the adaptive attack strategies we simulated exceeds the
bound
([Figure 4](#A1.F4 "In A.1 Federated-Tier Simulations at the Deployed Geometry ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

###### Safety with less verification effort.

In a 120-user community
([Figure 5](#A1.F5 "In A.1 Federated-Tier Simulations at the Deployed Geometry ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")),
reusing community-confirmed entries saves each user $`2.36`$ required
approvals on average ($`38\%`$) compared with verifying alone, and a
larger quorum provides substantial safety gains at a modest cost:
raising $`N`$ from $`3`$ to $`14`$ reduces the certified risk bound by a
factor of $`58`$ while adding only $`0.64`$ required approvals per user.

### 5 Self-Constructing the Knowledge Base

We test autonomous shared-knowledge construction on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench
telecom ([Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), with one construction run
per model and community size $`M\in\{12,24,60,90\}`$. A single model
family explores tasks, verifies extracted knowledge, and reviews shared
entries. Publication follows safety verification, sharability screening,
and consent to the exact content.

The protocol uses a promotion quorum $`N{=}10`$ and fixed dispute
thresholds $`k{=}31`$, $`m{=}20`$, and $`m_{\mathrm{rej}}{=}12`$. To
demonstrate the safety performance through PerMIT, we manually submitted
direct memory-injection payloads in crafted entries through
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench’s normal submission path. None of the 12 direct
memory-injection payloads reached the Community-Confirmed tier.

Utility uses 24 held-out tasks with two trials each and matched seeds
(48 paired episodes per arm).
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Self-Constructing the Knowledge Base ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
reports environment-completion scores (env_frac) and four-size pooled
task-cluster bootstrap intervals, conditional on the observed bases;

details the resampling.

Across $`M{=}12,24,60,90`$, the retained knowledge bases contain 3–7,
7–12, 30–40, and 45–64 entries respectively, across the three backbones.
Review effort per agent remains roughly level from 24 to 90 agents as
the shared stock grows. This supports the practical co-scaling pattern
of more reusable knowledge without proportional growth in individual
review effort.

At $`M{=}90`$, all means exceed the knowledge-free baseline; pooled
gains across community sizes survive three-backbone Holm correction for
Sonnet and Kimi, but not GLM-5. Kimi-built knowledge also improves a
zero-state Claude-Haiku-4.5 agent by $`+0.198`$ $`[+0.073,+0.333]`$ in a
separate 400-step, 48-episode evaluation (details in
Appendix [A.7](#A1.SS7 "A.7 Autonomous Telecom Construction: Methods and Additional Results ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

### 6 Conclusion and Future Directions

PerMIT contributes a finite memory interface with machine-checked
integrity guarantees, a federated protocol that turns exact-content
endorsements into reusable trust, and an autonomous workflow for
constructing useful shared knowledge. Under explicit assumptions, the
protocol bounds poison promotion and wrongful eviction while reducing
repeated verification. The agent communities promoted no direct
injection payloads and improved held-out task performance through
PerMIT.

These results motivate three future directions. First, provenance and
endorsement do not ensure usefulness: shared memory may contain
redundant, inaccurate, or hallucinated knowledge, motivating
quality-aware gates and active memory management. Second, estimating
rare promotion events required five billion simulated attempts and over
50 hours of computation; more efficient calibration with live verifiers
and users would strengthen deployment evidence. Third, adaptive payload
search against live verifiers remains an open empirical question. Our
simulations test the protocol’s conditional safety boundaries through
adaptive protocol attacks under controlled reviewer responses; they do
not replace adaptive payload search against live verifiers. Human or
agent memory managers could combine memories and review their joint
meaning and intended use, then seek fresh user endorsements of the
combined content before it becomes trusted. Testing this workflow
against adaptive endorsement and delayed-combination attacks is a future
direction. Matched component controls and measured human review effort
would further clarify deployment trade-offs.

#### A.2 The Trojan Hippo Benchmark in Brief

Trojan Hippo ([Das et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) evaluates persistent
memory poisoning under an indirect-injection threat model: the user is
trusted, the attacker controls only content the agent reads through its
tools, and the attacker’s goal is to exfiltrate sensitive user data to
an attacker-controlled address. The attack has two stages. In the
injection stage, a crafted inbound email read through a mailbox tool
carries a payload that the memory backend silently stores; in the
activation stage, after $`N`$ unrelated benign sessions, a user request
on a sensitive topic triggers the stored payload, which induces the
agent to send the user’s message to the attacker through an outbound
tool.
[Table 3](#A1.T3 "In Audit baselines. ‣ A.2 The Trojan Hippo Benchmark in Brief ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
summarizes the benchmark’s coverage and scale.

###### PerMIT live containment protocol.

PerMIT replaces the benchmark memory backend with its RLM reader and
confirmation interface. The four main-table backbones are served through
AWS Bedrock. Each case is placed in a fresh store as untrusted
email-tool output in an ingestion session and exercised from a
subsequent trigger session. The harness combines a live protected-agent
rollout with a targeted reader-to-tool probe: the reader fills an
address field, and the probe attempts to pass the resulting handle to
send_email, with an additional literal-address variant. This explicitly
attempts to exercise the action boundary without relying solely on the
planner to initiate exfiltration. A case succeeds if either executed
probe produces a recorded sink invocation whose serialized arguments
contain the benchmark attacker address. The probes run sequentially in
the same per-case store. In LLMVerifier mode, the reader probe also
performs retrieval-stage crystallization and confirmation. OpenGate
accepts every confirmation; OracleGate supplies the idealized
correct-user decisions; LLMVerifier uses the designated model. The
comparisons are between complete configurations.

###### Audit baselines.

Our A-MemGuard and LLM-Auditor reimplementations share the benchmark
retrieval path and reuse the corresponding undefended cases. A-MemGuard
cross-checks per-record reasoning chains and maintains a per-case lesson
store; LLM-Auditor independently audits each retrieved record. Retrieval
depth is $`K{=}8`$ for RAG and $`K{=}10`$ for Mem0. Both discard flagged
records; our auditor is a drop-only variant, not the rewriting auditor
described in the original work.

|  Aspect |  Benchmark specification |
|----|----|
|  Threat model |  Indirect injection only: the attacker controls the From, Subject, and Body of inbound email; cannot modify the agent’s code, system prompt, memory implementation, or user queries; is white-box with respect to prompt, backend, and tool interface but black-box with respect to model weights; and observes nothing but a successful exfiltration. |
|  Environment |  A tool-calling email assistant. read_all_emails and search_emails are the untrusted read tools; send_email, reply_to_email, and forward_to_email are the outbound tools through which exfiltration occurs. |
|  Trigger topics |  Finance, health, legal, tax, identity; user prompts are templated with sampled sensitive entities (account balances, diagnoses and medications, case details, W-2 figures, ID numbers). |
|  Attack generation |  OpenEvolve-style evolutionary search per (topic, backend, defense): an LLM mutator proposes payload variants, an agent-in-the-loop scorer checks exfiltration and an LLM critic scores 1–10, over a MAP-Elites diversity grid. One training case and four held-out test cases per (topic, backend), drawn from disjoint template and entity pools. |
|  Benign histories |  Multi-session, single-user conversation histories generated with a modified LoCoMo pipeline; the payload is injected before session $`N{=}0`$ and the trigger arrives after $`N`$ benign sessions. Undefended ASR does not decay up to $`N{=}100`$. |
|  Memory backends |  Context (sliding window); RAG (512-character chunks, top-8); Explicit (an update_memory list injected into the system prompt); Mem0 (LLM-extracted atomic facts, top-10); plus a no-memory control. |
|  Defenses |  User-prompt-only (index only user messages); No-untrusted-write (“No untrusted tools” in our tables: suppress memory writes after a read tool); Limit-memory-length (80-character entries); Provable policy (two-label IFC that taints a session on any read tool or tainted retrieval and blocks outbound tools in tainted sessions). Undefined pairs: User-prompt-only$`\times`$Explicit and Limit-memory-length$`\times`$Context. |
|  Utility |  Seven benign capability suites—memory_only, assistant_responses, untrusted_probe, disable_send, untrusted_send, memory_tools, long_memory—aggregated by arithmetic and harmonic mean; the harmonic mean collapses if any suite does. |
|  Reported strength |  Undefended ASR up to 85–100% on Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5-mini; the four defenses reduce ASR to 0–5% in most configurations, the provable policy to 0% everywhere at a harmonic-mean utility near zero. |

Table 3: Trojan Hippo at a glance ([Das et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)).

#### A.3 Implementation Gap in the Provable-Policy Baseline

In the supplied Trojan Hippo implementation, GLM-5 records 10% ASR under
the provable-policy baseline with both Explicit memory and Mem0 (two
successful attacks among twenty cases per configuration). The successful
cases are health/01 and legal/03 for Explicit, and finance/01 and
legal/03 for Mem0.

Our code audit identified inconsistent taint propagation in
search_emails: the tool marks the session untrusted in
SessionTrustManager but does not update the separate
ProvablePolicyManager state consulted by send_email. An untrusted search
can therefore leave the outbound guard’s trusted state unchanged. All
four successful traces exhibit the corresponding inconsistency: an
untrusted-read notification is followed by an outbound check with
is_trusted=True and will_block=False, and the benchmark’s outbox-based
attack checker reports success. These logs do not establish that the
successful sends were triggered by retrieval of poisoned
persistent-memory entries.

We retain the measured rates as results of the supplied benchmark
implementation. The observed failures illustrate a practical enforcement
gap: missing taint updates or inconsistent security state can permit
attacker-controlled content to induce disclosure despite an intended
information-flow restriction. Formal guarantees depend on faithful
implementation of their assumptions across all relevant execution paths;
these results expose a loophole in the evaluated enforcement rather than
a counterexample to the intended policy’s guarantee.

#### A.4 Additional Backbones and Serving Configurations

Three backbones are reported here rather than in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Setup. ‣ 4.1 The Single-User Tier ‣ 4 Results ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust").
Qwen-3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it were served locally under vLLM with a
common resource configuration (tensor parallelism over four GPUs,
32,768-token context, 0.92 GPU memory utilization, automatic tool
choice) and family-specific parsers. Qwen-3.6-27B:

> vllm serve --tensor-parallel-size 4 --max-model-len 32768
> --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --enable-auto-tool-choice
> --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3

Gemma-4-31B-it additionally requires a model-specific chat template and,
on our stack, the native sampler:

> VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 vllm serve --tensor-parallel-size 4
> --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92
> --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser
> gemma4 --chat-template tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja

Tool-call parsing on a self-hosted server is part of the measurement
rather than a detail of it, because a defence that mediates tool calls
is sensitive to how those calls are extracted from the model’s output,
and the parser is necessarily family-specific. The two backbones
therefore share a serving stack but not a parser or chat template: they
are comparable to each other at the stack level, not to the
Bedrock-served set of the main table, and the per-family parser and
template choices are recorded rather than left implicit. The lightweight
verifiers (Qwen-3.5-2B and Qwen-3.5-4B) were served under the same vLLM
stack, one GPU each, with a 16,384-token context, 0.90 GPU memory
utilization, the native sampler, and the family’s reasoning parser;
verifiers render verdicts rather than tool calls, so no tool-call parser
is involved. GPT-5.5 is served through the same Bedrock APIs as GPT-5.4.

Three readings the main table compresses are visible here. First, attack
success is zero in all twenty-eight cells, which is the only column with
no spread at all. Second, verifier size does not order the results: the
4B verifier has the higher harmonic mean on four of the seven backbones
and the lower one on three, its false-positive rate is lower on five,
and its two directions do not agree, since it wins by $`25.0`$ points of
HM on Qwen-3.6-27B and loses by $`17.0`$ on Kimi-K2.5. The two are
therefore better described as two draws from one quality tier than as a
size ladder, and a two-point size difference is not the axis to select
on. Third, the backbone matters more than the verifier. For a fixed
verifier the spread across backbones reaches $`18.3`$ points of AM and
$`45.1`$ of HM under the 2B model, while for a fixed backbone the spread
across the three model occupants reaches $`20`$ points of AM on
Kimi-K2.5. A deployment choosing a small verifier should therefore
validate it against its own backbone rather than against a published
ranking.

#### A.6 Domain Dependence of Self-Constructed Knowledge

We repeat the end-to-end autonomous construction experiment in the
banking domain of $`\tau^{2}`$-bench using the same three model
families.
Table [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ A.6 Domain Dependence of Self-Constructed Knowledge ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
reports the resulting held-out utility. Unlike the telecom experiment in
the main text, banking provides a golden-retrieval oracle rather than a
hand-written policy manual; because these reference conditions are not
directly comparable, the table reports the confirmatory contrast against
the knowledge-free baseline only.

| Backbone          | No knowledge | $`\bm{\Delta}`$ vs. no knowledge \[95% CI\] |
|-------------------|--------------|---------------------------------------------|
| GLM-5             | 0.428        | $`-0.000\;[-0.048,+0.048]`$                 |
| Kimi-K2.5         | 0.467        | $`+0.002\;[-0.027,+0.030]`$                 |
| Claude-Sonnet-4.6 | 0.590        | $`-0.015\;[-0.081,+0.045]`$                 |

Table 8: Utility of the autonomously constructed knowledge base in the
banking domain. Contrasts against the no-knowledge baseline are paired
by task and seed; intervals are 95% confidence intervals.

The self-constructed knowledge base produces no detectable utility gain
in banking: all confidence intervals include zero. This contrast with
telecom is consistent with the information available in the two
environments. Telecom tasks require causal, experience-derived knowledge
about how the environment behaves—knowledge that is absent from the
supplied documentation and can be acquired only through interaction.
Banking tasks primarily require locating information in a well-indexed
document corpus that the environment’s retrieval system already makes
available on demand. Consequently, the telecom community can contribute
knowledge that later agents would otherwise lack, whereas the banking
community largely distils information that each agent can already
retrieve independently. Together with GLM-5’s near-ceiling telecom
result, these findings identify a practical boundary on the utility of
shared memory: self-constructed knowledge is most valuable when it
captures scarce, experience-derived information, and least valuable when
the environment already supplies the required information or the
underlying agent has little remaining performance headroom.

#### A.7 Autonomous Telecom Construction: Methods and Additional Results

###### Construction and evaluation.

The construction ladder comprises one run for each of three model
families (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, GLM-5, and Kimi-K2.5) and four community
sizes $`M\in\{12,24,60,90\}`$. Each run uses one model family for all
construction roles. Agents crystallize session knowledge into an
untrusted handle, submit its exact content to the safety gate for
reasoning use, screen approved content for generality and privacy, and
consent to publication. Other agents then review shared entries.

The standard utility evaluation uses 24 held-out tasks with two trials
each (48 task/trial pairs per arm) and a 200-step limit. No Prior
Knowledge (A0) provides no shared knowledge base, PerMIT (A2) supplies
community-confirmed knowledge, and Expert Manual (A4) uses the
benchmark’s alternative hand-written workflow policy. A4 is not the
original policy with extra instructions appended, nor an oracle upper
bound on task performance. A0 and A2 keep prompts identical outside the
knowledge block. A2 includes all retained entries, with a coarse
ordering that distinguishes uncontested from vindicated entries, without
truncation. Generated experience primarily covers MMS troubleshooting;
the reported Sonnet and Kimi gains are concentrated in that task family.
This supports transfer of relevant experience, without establishing
gains for every task family.

###### Pairing and uncertainty.

Seeds are matched by task and trial across arms.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Self-Constructing the Knowledge Base ‣ Part I Main Paper ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
separates the $`M{=}90`$ means from the analysis pooled across all four
A2 community sizes against corresponding A0 episodes.
Table [9](#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Pairing and uncertainty. ‣ A.7 Autonomous Telecom Construction: Methods and Additional Results ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
gives the complete size ladder and repeats the pooled analysis for
reference. Pooling yields 192 paired differences but reuses the
evaluation tasks and baseline; these are not 192 independent tasks. The
analysis resamples whole tasks jointly across their trials and sizes:
95% confidence intervals use 10,000 cluster-bootstrap resamples, and the
continuous-score test uses 20,000 task-cluster sign-flip permutations,
both with analysis seed 20260811. Holm correction across the three
same-backbone comparisons gives adjusted $`p`$-values of $`0.0066`$ for
Claude-Sonnet-4.6, $`0.0325`$ for Kimi-K2.5, and $`0.9356`$ for GLM-5.
The bootstrap confidence intervals are pointwise, not
multiplicity-adjusted. Using $`m{=}5`$ as a conservative multiplicity
sensitivity analysis gives adjusted $`p{=}0.0110`$ for Sonnet and
$`p{=}0.0650`$ for Kimi. These quantify evaluation uncertainty for the
observed knowledge bases, not construction variability; pooled intervals
must not be read as $`M{=}90`$ intervals. Step-limit terminations
receive zero environment-completion score; infrastructure failures are
excluded from the common paired set and counted separately.

| Builder and agent | $`M{=}12`$ | $`M{=}24`$ | $`M{=}60`$ | $`M{=}90`$ |
|-------------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|
| Claude-Sonnet-4.6 | 0.7917     | 0.7431     | 0.8090     | 0.7986     |
| Kimi-K2.5         | 0.9375     | 0.9167     | 0.8750     | 0.8854     |
| GLM-5             | 0.9792     | 0.9583     | 0.9479     | 0.9688     |

| Builder and agent | Pooled PerMIT | Pooled $`\Delta`$ vs. A0 \[95% CI\] |
|-------------------|---------------|-------------------------------------|
| Claude-Sonnet-4.6 | 0.7856        | $`+0.1363\;[+0.0651,+0.2092]`$      |
| Kimi-K2.5         | 0.9037        | $`+0.1120\;[+0.0339,+0.1979]`$      |
| GLM-5             | 0.9635        | $`+0.0052\;[-0.0521,+0.0781]`$      |

Table 9: Same-backbone telecom utility across community sizes (upper
panel), and the separate four-size pooled paired analysis (lower panel).
Each size uses 48 task/trial pairs. Pooled 95% intervals use
task-cluster bootstrap resampling and do not describe the $`M{=}90`$
result alone.

###### Fixed geometry and finite review opportunities.

The construction ladder keeps $`N{=}10`$, $`k{=}31`$, $`m{=}20`$, and
$`m_{\mathrm{rej}}{=}12`$ fixed. The panel can terminate when a decision
threshold is reached; 31 votes are not required for every resolution.
Nevertheless, $`M{=}12`$ cannot supply 20 fresh accepting panelists, nor
the initiating rejection plus 12 further rejecting panelists required
for eviction. Entries can be detected and frozen without reaching either
terminal outcome. At $`M{=}24`$, early threshold resolution can be
feasible, subject to eligibility. Construction is sequential within one
epoch: an entry published by agent $`i`$ has at most $`M-i`$ later
reviewers. Raw promotion fractions therefore mix review quality with
available demand. From $`M{=}24`$ to 90, reviews per agent change from
13.92 to 14.27 for Sonnet, 9.58 to 7.16 for GLM-5, and 12.25 to 10.70
for Kimi, while evaluated knowledge grows from 7 to 48, 10 to 45, and 12
to 64 entries, respectively. This is a finite-scale knowledge/effort
trade-off, not a monotonic task-performance trend or an asymptotic
theorem. At matched remaining-review horizon $`H{=}30`$, benign yield
from $`M{=}60`$ to 90 is 0.833 to 0.833, 0.824 to 1.000, and 0.826 to
0.976 for Sonnet, GLM-5, and Kimi, respectively; one run per setting
limits inference about population effects.

###### Unfiltered shared-knowledge control.

The existing A1 arm supplies shared knowledge without the
community-promotion filter.
Table [10](#A1.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Unfiltered shared-knowledge control. ‣ A.7 Autonomous Telecom Construction: Methods and Additional Results ‣ Appendix A Additional Results ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
compares A1 and A2 at the same $`M{=}90`$ construction budget, rather
than comparing A1 to the four-size pooled result. A1 has higher mean
utility on all three backbones. These are descriptive comparisons: the
retained contents and prompt lengths differ, and a paired A1–A2 test is
not reported here. This is a benign-utility comparison, not a
measurement of relative attack resistance. It establishes that
unfiltered shared experience can help; it does not isolate the promotion
filter on identical candidate pools or substitute for a simpler voting
control.

| GLM-5             | 0.5638      | $`+0.0957\;[-0.056,+0.261]`$   |
| Kimi-K2.5         | 0.6064      | $`+0.1383\;[+0.0222,+0.2660]`$ |

No Prior Knowledge (A0) is 0.4681 and Expert Manual is 0.5319 for this
set. The 400-step Kimi result is reported separately in the text.

###### Scope of the safety probes.

The separate 12-payload direct memory-injection campaign reports no
community promotion. This endpoint concerns access to the shared fast
path; it does not measure personal acceptance, use before promotion, or
every intermediate lifecycle transition.

#### B.1 Operations and the reply alphabet

Every reply the interpreter returns to $`P`$ is drawn from a fixed
alphabet
(Rule [R10](#Thmrulex10 "Rule R10 (Constant-alphabet interface, with totality). ‣ S2.3 Interface rules ‣ Appendix S2 Formal Specification of the Memory Interface ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")),

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r\;::=\;\mathsf{ack}\;\mid\;h_{j}\;\mid\;\mathsf{fail}\;\mid\;\mathsf{dec}(\mathsf{accept})\;\mid\;\mathsf{dec}(\mathsf{reject})\;\mid\;\mathsf{bytes}(b),\ b\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{E}},
``` |  |

so the only readable text $`P`$ ever receives is the verbatim content of
a trusted block. The isolation half of the single-user argument
(Lemma [D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma D.1 (Protected-agent isolation). ‣ Assumptions and boundaries. ‣ D.1 Interface and trust assumptions ‣ Appendix D Formal Guarantees and Proof Sketches ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"))
is the check, operation by operation, that untrusted bytes never appear
in the last category;
[Table 12](#A2.T12 "In B.1 Operations and the reply alphabet ‣ Appendix B The Memory Interface in Practice ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
makes that check readable. Two further properties keep the alphabet
uninformative about untrusted memory: handle identifiers are fixed by
$`P`$’s own operation sequence and never encode store contents
(Rule [R1](#Thmrulex1 "Rule R1 (Operation-determined naming: handles and block identifiers). ‣ S2.3 Interface rules ‣ Appendix S2 Formal Specification of the Memory Interface ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")),
and an empty search, a reader failure, and an unoccupied identifier all
return the same operation-determined handle
(Rules [R6](#Thmrulex6 "Rule R6 (Null handle). ‣ S2.3 Interface rules ‣ Appendix S2 Formal Specification of the Memory Interface ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"), [R7](#Thmrulex7 "Rule R7 (Failure indistinguishability). ‣ S2.3 Interface rules ‣ Appendix S2 Formal Specification of the Memory Interface ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")).

#### B.2 Label lifecycle

Blocks are immutable once written
(Assumptions [A1](#Thmassumptionx1 "Assumption A1 (Deterministic source labelling). ‣ S2.4 Trust axioms ‣ Appendix S2 Formal Specification of the Memory Interface ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")–[A2](#Thmassumptionx2 "Assumption A2 (Label persistence and block immutability). ‣ S2.4 Trust axioms ‣ Appendix S2 Formal Specification of the Memory Interface ‣ Part III Complete Formal Development ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust"));
trust changes only by the creation of a fresh block.
[Figure 6](#A2.F6 "In B.2 Label lifecycle ‣ Appendix B The Memory Interface in Practice ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
shows every permitted transition. The only path from $`\mathsf{U}`$ to a
trusted label is $`\mathsf{display}`$ followed by an accepting
$`\mathsf{confirm}`$, which copies the displayed bytes into a new
$`\mathsf{C}`$ block and leaves the untrusted original in place.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: Label lifecycle. No other transition exists: no operation
relabels a block in place, and $`\mathsf{CC}`$ status lives in the
shared tier rather than in any local store.

#### B.3 A worked trace: dormant poison across two sessions

[Table 13](#A2.T13 "In B.3 A worked trace: dormant poison across two sessions ‣ Appendix B The Memory Interface in Practice ‣ Part II Empirical and Explanatory Appendices ‣ PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agentsvia Machine-Checked Integrity Theoremsand Scalable Community Trust")
follows a Trojan Hippo-style episode: a payload planted through one
untrusted tool call in session 1 and activated by a sensitive request in
session 2. The third column is the point of the exercise—it lists
everything $`P`$ ever receives.
````
